title: Fostering the Future for American Children and Families
summary:
This executive order sets out to upgrade the foster care system and give children and young adults in or leaving foster care a clearer path to stability, education, and work. It calls for better use of data and technology, faster and safer placements, and new partnerships—especially a “Fostering the Future” effort that includes an online hub to connect people with housing, health, school, jobs, and mentoring.

Who stands to benefit? Children and teens in foster care could see quicker investigations, fewer placement disruptions, and more permanent homes. Young adults aging out of care may gain easier access to scholarships, short-term job training, and tools that build financial independence. Foster and adoptive families could get better support and matching, which may reduce burnout. Caseworkers might see simpler, more modern systems and less busywork. States could gain clearer feedback from annual scorecards and technical help to modernize their systems. Communities, schools, and employers may also benefit from a stronger pipeline of prepared, supported young adults.

Who might be negatively affected? Expanding the use of data-driven tools, including systems that predict risks, raises concerns about privacy and the chance that mistakes or bias could harm families. The order pushes agencies to remove barriers that keep faith-based groups from taking part, which supporters say widens the pool of caregivers. Others worry this could conflict with local non-discrimination rules and limit options for some prospective parents or youth. Smaller providers, especially those without strong tech resources, may struggle to keep up with new expectations. Even with promises to cut low-value reporting, states could feel pressure from public scorecards that oversimplify complex cases. And shifting unspent federal funds into new priorities could leave some existing programs with fewer resources.

What to watch: new rules and tools over the next six months, the launch of the online platform, and the first state scorecards. The impact will depend on how safeguards, civil rights protections, and community input are built into the rollout.
